The Seneca Falls Convention. In July of 1848, about 300 people gathered in Seneca Falls, New York for the foundational meeting of the American women's rights movement, including men who supported women's equality. Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott organized the convention, two activists who had been excluded from speaking at the 1840 World Anti-Slavery Convention in London. They produced the Declaration of Sentiments, modeled on the Declaration of Independence, asserting that all men and women are created equal with inalienable rights. The convention explicitly demanded woman suffrage, the right to vote, a radical claim at the time that even many sympathetic observers thought too extreme or impossible. The convention articulated grievances against laws that made women civilly and legally inferior, including marriage laws that stripped women of rights, property restrictions, denial of education, and complete political voicelessness. Beyond voting rights, it addressed issues of women's bodily autonomy, employment, divorce rights, and education, showing the breadth of feminist demands. Susan B. Anthony did not attend, but she quickly became a leading organizer of the subsequent women's rights movement, partnering with Stanton for decades. The convention established women's suffrage as the central goal of American feminism for the next seven decades until the Nineteenth Amendment finally granted voting rights to women in 1920.
